scenes.title: Recursive Queries: Hierarchies & Graph Traversal
scenes.narration: Recursive common table expressions let a single query walk through hierarchical and graph-shaped data by repeatedly referencing itself until there is nothing left to expand.

scenes.title: When you reach for recursion
bullets: Org charts where employees report to managers who report to other managers
Category trees such as nested product taxonomies of arbitrary depth
Graph edges like friend-of-friend links or dependency chains
Anything where the depth of nesting is unknown ahead of time
scenes.narration: Reach for recursion when a table references itself and the depth is unknown. Org charts chain employees to managers to their managers in turn. Category trees nest arbitrarily deep, so a fixed number of joins cannot cover them. Graph edges like social connections or dependency chains need the same repeated expansion. In every case you cannot predict how many levels exist, which is exactly what recursion handles.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a recursive CTE
steps: Anchor member: the starting rows, e.g. the root node
UNION ALL joins anchor results with the recursive step
Recursive member: references the CTE to find the next level
Repeat until the recursive member returns no new rows
scenes.narration: A recursive CTE has two halves joined by UNION ALL. The anchor member selects the starting rows, typically the root of the tree. The recursive member then references the CTE itself, joining it to the base table to fetch the next level down. The database keeps re-running that recursive step, feeding each new batch back in, and stops automatically once no new rows are produced.

scenes.title: Traversing an org chart from the CEO
scenes.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    -- anchor: start at the top of the hierarchy
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- recursive: find people reporting to the current level
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT depth, name
FROM org
ORDER BY depth, name;
scenes.narration: Here we walk an org chart starting from the CEO. The anchor selects the employee whose manager is null, the top of the tree, and labels it depth one. UNION ALL then feeds those rows into the recursive member, which joins the employees table to the CTE so every employee whose manager appears in the current level is pulled in at depth plus one. The engine repeats this until nobody new reports upward, giving us the full tree with each person's level.

scenes.title: Graph traversal with cycle protection
scenes.code:
WITH RECURSIVE reachable AS (
    SELECT src, dst,
           ARRAY[src, dst] AS path
    FROM edges
    WHERE src = 'A'

    UNION ALL

    SELECT r.src, e.dst,
           r.path || e.dst
    FROM edges e
    JOIN reachable r ON e.src = r.dst
    -- stop if we would revisit a node
    WHERE e.dst <> ALL(r.path)
)
SELECT dst, path
FROM reachable;
scenes.narration: Graphs can contain cycles, so naive recursion could loop forever. This query traverses edges starting at node A and carries a path array recording every node visited. The recursive member appends each newly reached node to that path. The crucial guard is the where clause: it only follows an edge when the destination is not already in the path, so the traversal refuses to revisit a node and the query terminates safely.

scenes.text: Always give a recursive CTE a stopping condition. For trees the structure ends naturally; for graphs, track the visited path and skip nodes you have already seen to avoid infinite loops.
scenes.narration: The one thing to always get right is termination. Trees end on their own, but graphs need an explicit cycle check, so track the path you have walked and refuse to re-enter a node you have already visited.
